title: Most Strongly Supported
summary: Like Must Be True, but the answer only has to be well supported. Prefer modest, hedged claims that stay close to the facts.

slides.title: Modest wins
body: The right answer doesn’t have to be certain, but it has to be closely backed by the facts. In practice that means it is usually cautious: “may”, “some”, “not necessarily”.
Wrong answers overreach: they turn a correlation into a cause, some into most, or one case into a rule.
slides.callout: When two choices both fit, take the one that claims less.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
The information above provides the most support for which one of the following?

steps.label: Collect the facts
steps.do: Read everything as true. Note any comparisons, numbers and causal-sounding phrases.

steps.label: Ask what’s safe
steps.do: What could you say about these facts that no reasonable reader would dispute?

steps.label: Check the strength
steps.do: Kill choices that claim causes, certainty, or quantities the facts don’t reach.

steps.label: Choose the safest
steps.do: Between survivors, prefer the more hedged one.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.stimulus: In a long-term study of office workers, those who took a short walk after lunch reported fewer afternoon headaches than those who stayed at their desks. The walkers also drank, on average, more water during the afternoon.
slides.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Walking after lunch prevents afternoon headaches.
choices.B: Drinking more water is the main reason the walkers had fewer headaches.
choices.C: Office workers who stay at their desks drink no water in the afternoon.
choices.D: Something other than the walking itself may account for some of the difference in headaches.
choices.E: Most office workers get afternoon headaches.

steps.label: Fact one
steps.note: Walkers reported fewer headaches. A correlation, not a cause.
steps.highlight: reported fewer afternoon headaches than those who stayed at their desks

steps.label: Fact two
steps.note: Walkers also drank more water. A second difference between the groups.
steps.highlight: The walkers also drank, on average, more water during the afternoon.

steps.label: What’s safe
steps.note: We can’t say which difference matters, only that walking may not be the whole story.

why.A: Too strong: a correlation does not show walking prevents headaches.
why.B: Too strong: water is a possible factor, not shown to be the main one.
why.C: Extreme: the facts say walkers drank more, not that others drank none.
why.D: Correct. Water intake is a second difference between the groups, so something besides walking may explain part of the gap.
why.E: Nothing tells us how common headaches are.

traps.name: Cause from correlation
traps.tell: The facts show two things together; the choice says one causes the other.

traps.name: Upgraded quantity
traps.tell: Some becomes most, more becomes all, fewer becomes none.

traps.name: One case to a rule
traps.tell: A single study or example becomes a general law.

traps.name: Comparison not made
traps.tell: Compares groups or times the facts never compared.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Supported, not certain, but close to the facts.
Hedged wording is a good sign here.
Prefer the choice that claims less.
